== F. The timing (design §7.1; P2b.2b.2c.2c design §5.3): ms from the mallet's first contact; the croqueted ball first moving (shifted by 0.2000 mm), the mallet's first contact ending, the ball–ball interval's end (the ball leaving), any second face interval; the model beside Fig. 4's research reading and re-reading (reference/sources/README.md:594-619), each ±0.5 frame on Gugan's own "a frame or two" (one frame 0.1250 ms). The model twice: "law" from the contact law's intervals, "video" as Gugan 4's video would time it, a contact on while the two bodies' surfaces are within 0.2000 mm of touching (the face's separation from the striker's ball, the balls' gap). Every video clock starts at first touch, as Fig. 4 times every event from the mallet's first contact (gate stage 1's ruling A1): the impact begins with the face touching, so the approach before it is not simulated, and the video and the camera prepend it analytically, the face's separation (−t)·U for t < 0 (U the head's speed along aim at the impact's start), the balls at rest at their gap, from first touch at t = −shift/U (0.1042 ms before the impact at C3S's U and 0.2000 mm). The camera samples that run at 8,000 fps, at 16 frame phases evenly spaced over one frame from first touch, so that every phase's first frame shows the contact (cameraIntervals' precondition); its times are whole frames from that first frame, each the range over the phases, at 0.2000, 0.4000, 0.6000 mm (design §7.9), and a release no frame shows is marked UNSEEN. A second face interval counts only if it begins within the strike's window; 'on' marks a contact still seen at the impact's end. A stroke whose three bodies stay loaded throughout is reported, not failed (decision 5) ==

-- F.2 the sources (design §5.3's table), each seen by its own instrument above --
Gugan 4 (2009): the CA's film, 8,000 fps; "all straight two-ball croquet strokes are double taps"; C3S touching shows a release
CA, "Croquet Dynamics" (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/video/): the CA team's reading of the same film; "cases where balls started quite close to one another did not show double taps as the mallet and strikers ball were still in contact when contact was made with the second ball"
Plummer, "Multiple Taps in Croquet Strokes" (2000), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/multiple/: electrical contact, 5 µs a point, 2.65 V through 82 kΩ; departures: 0.02 mm of aluminium foil glued to a Permali face, Jaques Eclipse balls thickly sprayed with graphite, played indoors on a carpet; "Single ball strokes and most croquet strokes showed no sign of multiple contacts"; in-line stops 1.8 (soft) and 2.0 ms (hard), in-line drives 1.4 and 1.3 ms
Hall, "When a Mallet Strikes a Ball" (1994), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/hall/: electrical contact, no voltage given; departures: "a few strands of copper wire were wound around the ball", "a strip of aluminium foil was fixed to the ball", "Foil was also taped to the end faces of the mallet", and long strokes stopped "by a cushion"; ball 2 leaves "at about 1.8ms. The mallet remained in contact with ball 1 for a further period of 1.1 ms" (about 2.9 ms)

== P. The camera threshold's reach (design §7.9): VISIBLE_SHIFT is 0.2 mm, Gugan 4's resolution on paper. The thresholds read are exactly those P_INPUTS names (mm=path), each a section E output from a throwaway copy whose laws I.0 re-set at that threshold (SHIFT), the video's clock from first touch (gate stage 1's ruling A1); a threshold I.0 could not convert has no E run and no line here.
